doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: The skipped generation: mentoring from Danny Barker to Trombone Shorty
summary: He says kids now do not learn at the feet of older musicians. Shannon Powell, Herlin Riley, Wynton Marsalis and Trombone Shorty recall mentors such as Danny Barker, Cie Frazier and Tuba Fats.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: with drumsticks and you can still see a high school kid walking down the street home from school with a sousaphone wrapped around his head. So you don’t see that every day in other cities. I know it’s not true. But I see it. I mean maybe I don’t see it every day but yeah, every day I can see some evidence that yeah, there is music here happening. Now do we want the paradigm to be the brass band playing funky music? I mean in some of these music programs we have whole marching bands and there is only a handful of kids that can actually read music. So I don’t necessarily want that to be the only paradigm. I think we owe it to them to give them more proper music instruction, more traditional music instruction if you will. I think they should all know how to read music. I think the older musicians and the college students, they need to be taking more responsibility for mentoring the little kids and our primary school and our middle school kids. I think the high school kids could even have that role, that continuum of that mentoring tradition has been lost. I don’t think the musicians that you heard are following the professional bands around. I don’t think that they’ve gone and taken music lessons with Wendell Brunious, the trumpet players that you heard in this band. Well he doesn’t live in New Orleans now anyway, he lives in Sweden, but when he was around, I don’t think they were going to him. Shannon Powell is right there in the Treme across the street from Armstrong Park, and I don’t think kids are coming to him all the time for drum lessons. So it goes both ways. There is a tradition but at the same time it’s not, there’s a generation that’s been skipped. When I talk to Shannon Powell or Herlin Riley or any of the musicians, or even if you talk to Wynton Marsalis, they will tell you about the mentoring that they had from the professional musicians that grew up around them or that they had exposure to. They’ll talk about Danny Barker. Shannon will talk about Cié Frazier. Herlin will talk about musicians in his church. So that generation of musicians, who are maybe just a little bit older than me, still remember when they followed people around and that was how they got schooled in music. Leroi Jones will talk about the Fairview Baptist Church and even musicians a little bit younger than me like “Trombone Shorty” Andrews. If you got it out of him he would tell you about Anthony “Tuba Fats” Lacen. He would tell you about how he did have musicians in this community who were telling him how to get his shit together. So I think when you see a brass band of young kids I think you can recognize that there is definitely aspects of the musical tradition because of the exposure that they’ve had but I won’t say that they’ve had the same — I won’t say that the tradition is such that they actually learned their craft at the feet of older musicians.
